headline: UK and EU strike post-Brexit reset deal in Brussels, with food, carbon and youth mobility agreements but university fees unresolved

terms.meaning: A shared set of food, animal and plant health rules, so fewer border checks are needed.
An EU charge on carbon-heavy imports such as steel.
The EU zone where goods and services move freely under shared rules.

levels.headline: UK and EU strike post-Brexit reset deal in Brussels, with food, carbon and youth mobility agreements but university fees unresolved
levels.body:
Prime Minister Andy Burnham and EU leaders agreed a package at a summit in Brussels on 20 November. It covers a common agri-food area, a youth experience scheme and a deal on carbon markets. The government estimates it could add up to 0.5% to UK GDP by 2040, around £17 billion a year.
Under the food agreement, the UK and EU would apply the same sanitary and phytosanitary rules, ending routine checks on products such as dairy and eggs and making pet travel easier. The carbon deal exempts £6.5 billion of British exports, including steel and aluminium, from the EU's Carbon Border Adjustment Mechanism.
The youth scheme would let 100,000 people aged 18 to 31 from each side live, work or study in the other's territory for up to three years, without access to benefits. First travel is due no later than January 2030. University fees were not settled and should be concluded within six months.
Nigel Farage accused Burnham of betraying Brexit voters. Burnham says Brexit has not worked and plans a national conversation on the long-term relationship. The government says the deals need no payments into the EU budget.
levels.why: It reshapes how easily British firms trade with their largest market and reopens the argument over Brexit.

levels.headline: UK and EU agree reset deal on food, carbon and young people's travel
levels.body:
Prime Minister Andy Burnham struck a deal with the European Union at a summit in Brussels on Friday 20 November. It covers food and farming trade, carbon markets and a scheme for young people to live and work abroad. The government says it could be worth up to £17 billion a year to the UK economy by 2040.
Routine checks on many food and farm products moving between Britain and the EU would end, because both sides would follow the same rules. British steel and aluminium exports worth £6.5 billion would avoid the EU's carbon border charge.
Young people aged 18 to 31 could live, work or study in the other's territory for up to three years, with 100,000 places each way. The first trips are due by January 2030. A row over university fees for EU students remains and talks should finish within six months.
Nigel Farage called the deal a betrayal of Brexit. Burnham says Brexit has not worked, and the government says it will not pay into the EU budget.
levels.why: It is the biggest change to the UK's EU relationship in years and will be argued over for months.

levels.headline: UK and EU agree package on food, carbon and youth travel
levels.body:
The UK and the European Union have agreed a reset deal at a summit in Brussels. Prime Minister Andy Burnham signed up to three main measures, and the government says the package could lift the economy by up to 0.5% by 2040, around £17 billion a year.
First, the two sides will share rules on food and farming, so most routine checks at the border will go. Second, British exports of steel and aluminium worth £6.5 billion will be spared a new EU charge on carbon-heavy imports. Third, 100,000 young people aged 18 to 31 from each side will be able to live, work or study in the other place for up to three years.
Nothing was agreed on cheaper university fees for EU students. The two sides have six months to try.
Nigel Farage says the deal betrays Brexit voters. Mr Burnham says Brexit has not worked as promised and wants a national debate on the future relationship.
levels.why: It affects prices, jobs and travel, and it changes what Brexit means in practice.

levels.headline: Burnham agrees EU reset deal on food, carbon and youth schemes
levels.body:
Andy Burnham has agreed a post-Brexit reset deal with the European Union at a summit in Brussels. The prime minister says it will cut costs for British businesses and shoppers and open opportunities for young people. The government puts the benefit at up to £17 billion a year by 2040.
The agreement ends many routine border checks on food and farm goods by aligning British and EU rules. It also protects £6.5 billion of UK steel and aluminium exports from an EU carbon charge. A youth scheme will let 18 to 31-year-olds live and work in each other's territories for up to three years.
The question of lower university fees for EU students was left for further talks over the next six months.
Reform UK leader Nigel Farage accused Mr Burnham of betraying Brexit voters. The government insists the deal will not require payments to the EU budget.
levels.why: It could make trade with Europe cheaper and easier, but critics say it undoes parts of Brexit.

levels.headline: Prime minister agrees new deal with the EU on food, carbon and young people
levels.body:
Prime Minister Andy Burnham has made a new deal with the European Union. It was agreed at a meeting in Brussels on Friday. The government says it could add up to £17 billion a year to the UK economy by 2040.
The deal has three main parts. One is about food. Britain and the EU will use the same rules for food and farming, which means fewer checks at the border. Another protects British steel and aluminium sellers from a new EU tax on goods made with a lot of carbon. The last lets people aged 18 to 31 live, work or study in Europe, and Europeans in the UK, for up to three years.
Cheaper university fees for EU students were not agreed. Talks will continue for six months.
Nigel Farage says the deal betrays Brexit voters. The prime minister says Brexit has not worked as promised.
levels.why: It could lower some prices and give young people new choices, but not everyone agrees with it.

levels.headline: UK and EU agree new deal on food, carbon and travel for young people
levels.body:
The UK government has agreed a new deal with the European Union. This is a big step in how Britain and its closest neighbours work together after Brexit. The prime minister, Andy Burnham, says it will help to keep prices down.
The deal means less paperwork for food and farm goods crossing the Channel, because both sides will follow the same safety rules. Steel and aluminium made in Britain will not face a new EU charge on products that cause a lot of pollution. Young people aged 18 to 31 will be able to live, work or study in the other place for up to three years.
University fees for EU students are still being argued over. The two sides have six months to agree.
Some people, including Nigel Farage, say the deal goes against what Brexit voters wanted.
levels.why: It may change what you pay for food and what young people can do, and people disagree about it.

levels.headline: Britain and the EU make a new deal about food, travel and pollution rules
levels.body:
Britain has made a new deal with the European Union, a group of European countries. The UK left the EU in 2020, and since then trade between them has had more rules and more checks. The new deal will remove some of those.
Food and farm goods will have fewer checks at the border. That should make some foods cheaper and easier to sell. Young people aged 18 to 31 will be able to live and work in the other place for up to three years. British steel will not face an extra EU charge on pollution.
One thing is not settled yet. That is how much EU students should pay to study at British universities. The two sides will keep talking for six months.
Some people, like Nigel Farage, are angry about the deal. Others think it will help ordinary people.
levels.why: It could affect shop prices and holidays, and it shows how the UK now deals with its neighbours.

levels.headline: Britain and Europe agree to make trade and travel easier
levels.body:
Britain has agreed a deal with Europe. Britain used to be in the European Union, or EU. It left in 2020. After that, selling things between Britain and Europe got harder.
Now some of that will get easier. Food will face fewer checks at the border. This could help shops and farmers. Young people aged 18 to 31 will be able to live and work in Europe for up to three years. Young Europeans will be able to do the same in Britain.
Some things are not agreed yet. One is how much students from Europe should pay to go to British universities. The leaders will talk about it for six months.
Not everyone is happy. A politician called Nigel Farage says the deal is wrong. The prime minister, Andy Burnham, says it will help people.
levels.why: It could make some things cheaper and give young people new chances.

levels.headline: Britain and Europe say yes to a new deal
levels.body:
Britain has made a new deal with its neighbours in Europe. A deal is when two sides agree to a plan. Britain used to be part of a group of European countries called the EU, but it left. Since then, it has been harder to send things across the sea.
Now the rules will be easier. Food will not be checked as much when it comes in or goes out. That helps shops. Young people aged 18 to 31 will be able to go and live or work in Europe for a few years. Young people from Europe can come here too.
Some people do not like the deal. They think Britain should keep to the old plan. The prime minister, Andy Burnham, thinks the new deal will help.
levels.why: It could make life a bit easier and cheaper for lots of people.

levels.headline: Britain and its neighbours agree to share rules
levels.body:
Imagine two schools that stopped sharing a playground. Now it is hard to play together. Britain and the European Union are like those two schools. They stopped sharing some rules a few years ago.
This week the leaders agreed to share some rules again. That means food can cross the sea with fewer checks. Young people aged 18 to 31 can go and live in each other's places for up to three years, like going on a long trip to a new school.
The leaders have not agreed everything. They still need to decide how much students from Europe pay to go to British universities.
Some grown-ups are happy about the deal and some are cross. The prime minister is called Andy Burnham. He says it will help families.
levels.why: It could make shopping and travel easier, and grown-ups are still talking about it.

headline: S&P 500 closes down 3.7% on Friday, Dow and S&P in correction as AI sell-off deepens

terms.meaning: A fall of 10% or more from a recent peak.
A gauge of how nervous investors are about swings in share prices.
An index of 500 large US companies, a common measure of the US stock market.

levels.headline: S&P 500 closes down 3.7% on Friday, Dow and S&P in correction as AI sell-off deepens
levels.body:
The S&P 500 closed down on Friday 20 November, the last completed session, falling 3.7% to 6,910.39. The Dow Jones Industrial Average lost 949.73 points, or 1.93%, to 48,147.33. The Nasdaq Composite fell 5.28% to 22,617.73, which wiped out its gain for 2026.
Both the S&P 500 and the Dow ended more than 10% below their record closes, which is a market correction. For the week, the Dow fell 8%, its worst week since March 2020, and the S&P 500 fell 8.6%, its worst since April 2025. The Nasdaq lost about 10%.
Nvidia dropped 14% after a Reuters report that the US Securities and Exchange Commission is looking at its accounting. AMD fell more than 13%. CNBC also pointed to the Anthropic share listing, with investors cashing in on AI gains, and to worries that high inflation could push the Federal Reserve to raise rates again. The VIX fear gauge rose above 30.
levels.why: A fall this size hits pension funds and savings and can signal wider doubts about AI and interest rates.

levels.headline: Wall Street ends sharply lower: S&P 500 down 3.7%, Dow down 1.9%, Nasdaq down 5.3%
levels.body:
US shares fell sharply on Friday 20 November, the latest completed session. The S&P 500 closed down 3.7% at 6,910.39. The Dow Jones Industrial Average fell 1.93% to 48,147.33, and the Nasdaq Composite dropped 5.28% to 22,617.73, erasing its 2026 gains.
The S&P 500 and the Dow are now both more than 10% below their record highs, which traders call a correction. The Dow lost 8% over the week, its worst since March 2020, and the S&P 500 lost 8.6%.
Chipmaker Nvidia fell 14% after a report that US regulators are examining its accounting, and AMD fell more than 13%. Analysts also blamed profit-taking after the Anthropic share launch and fears that inflation will force more US interest rate rises. The VIX, a measure of market fear, went above 30.
levels.why: It shows how nervous investors are about artificial intelligence companies and rising interest rates.

levels.headline: US shares tumble: S&P 500 closes 3.7% lower, Nasdaq down more than 5%
levels.body:
US stock markets fell hard on Friday 20 November, the last full trading day. The S&P 500 closed down 3.7% at 6,910.39. The Dow Jones average fell 1.93% to 48,147.33. The tech-heavy Nasdaq lost 5.28%, closing at 22,617.73, and is now lower for the year.
The S&P 500 and Dow have each dropped more than 10% from their record highs, a move known as a correction. It was the Dow's worst week since March 2020, with an 8% fall.
Nvidia shares fell 14% after reports that the US financial regulator is examining its accounting, and AMD lost more than 13%. Investors are also worried that high inflation will push the Federal Reserve to raise interest rates again, and some sold after the much-hyped Anthropic stock market debut.
levels.why: Falling markets can hit pensions and savings and often signal worries about the wider economy.

levels.headline: Wall Street slumps as AI shares are sold off
levels.body:
The main US share indexes fell sharply on Friday 20 November, the last full session. The S&P 500 closed down 3.7% at 6,910.39. The Dow Jones Industrial Average lost 1.93% to 48,147.33, and the Nasdaq dropped 5.28% to 22,617.73.

levels.headline: US stock markets fall sharply as worries about AI grow
levels.body:
US share prices fell a lot on Friday 20 November, the last day the markets were open. The S&P 500, which tracks 500 big companies, closed down 3.7% at 6,910.39. The Dow Jones index lost 1.93% and ended at 48,147.33. The Nasdaq, which has many tech firms, fell 5.28% to 22,617.73.

levels.headline: Shares in the US drop as investors worry about AI companies
levels.body:
Share prices in the United States fell sharply on Friday 20 November. That was the last day markets were open. The S&P 500 index, which follows 500 large firms, closed down 3.7%. It ended at 6,910.39. The Dow Jones index fell 1.93% to 48,147.33. The Nasdaq fell 5.28% to 22,617.73.

levels.headline: US shares fall sharply on worries about AI and prices

US share prices fell a lot on Friday 20 November, the last day markets were open. The S&P 500, which follows 500 big companies, fell 3.7% and ended at 6,910.39. The Dow Jones index fell 1.93% to 48,147.33. The Nasdaq fell 5.28% to 22,617.73.

levels.headline: American share prices fall a lot

A share is a small piece of a company. People buy and sell shares on a stock market. Prices go up and down every day. On Friday 20 November they went down a lot in the United States. That was the last day the markets were open.

levels.headline: Share prices in America fell on Friday

A stock market is a place where people buy and sell tiny parts of companies. These parts are called shares. On Friday 20 November, share prices in America went down by a lot.
One list of 500 big companies, called the S&P 500, went down 3.7%. Another list, the Dow, went down 1.93%. A third, the Nasdaq, went down 5.28%.

levels.headline: Prices of company shares dropped in America
levels.body:
Think of a share as a tiny slice of a big pizza company. If lots of people want a slice, the price goes up. If lots of people want to sell their slices, the price goes down.
On Friday 20 November, lots of people in America wanted to sell. The S&P 500, a list of 500 big companies, fell 3.7%. Another list, called the Dow, fell 1.93%. A third, called the Nasdaq, fell 5.28%.
Many of the companies that fell make computer chips or AI. One of them, Nvidia, lost 14%. Grown-ups were worried that things in shops cost more and that borrowing money might cost more too. When they are worried, they sell. That is why prices dropped.

headline: UK inflation rises to 3.6% in October, a 12-month high, as motor fuel costs surge

terms.meaning: The rate at which prices rise over time.
Inflation leaving out food and energy, which swing a lot.
The Consumer Prices Index, the main official measure of UK inflation.

levels.headline: UK inflation rises to 3.6% in October, a 12-month high, as motor fuel costs surge
levels.body:
UK consumer price inflation rose to 3.6% in the year to October 2026, its highest level in 12 months, according to figures reported on 18 November. Economists had expected 3.7%, so the reading was slightly below forecast.
Rising fuel prices were the main driver. Motor fuel inflation reached its highest rate since July 2022, and diesel hit a record high. The jump is linked to energy costs after the conflict in the Middle East. Core inflation, which strips out volatile items such as energy and food, was unchanged at 2.8%.
The figure matters because the Bank of England, which raised its base rate to 4% on 5 November, is trying to bring inflation back down. The Bank has forecast that inflation could approach 5% by the middle of 2027. Analysts say another rate rise at the next meeting on 17 December remains possible.
levels.why: Higher inflation squeezes household budgets and keeps interest rates high.

levels.headline: UK inflation climbs to 3.6%, the highest in a year, driven by petrol and diesel
levels.body:
Prices across the UK rose 3.6% in the year to October, the fastest pace for 12 months. Economists had forecast 3.7%, so it was a touch lower than expected.
The biggest push came from fuel. Petrol and diesel rose at the fastest rate since July 2022, and diesel reached a record price. The rise follows higher energy costs linked to the war in the Middle East. Core inflation, which leaves out energy and food prices because they change so quickly, stayed at 2.8%.
The data will be watched closely by the Bank of England, which lifted interest rates to 4% earlier this month. It expects inflation to near 5% by mid-2027. Some analysts expect another rise on 17 December.
levels.why: It affects the cost of living and whether mortgages and loans get more expensive.

levels.headline: Inflation rises to 3.6% as petrol and diesel prices climb
levels.body:
Prices in the UK were 3.6% higher in October than a year earlier. That is the highest rate in a year. Forecasters had expected 3.7%, so it was slightly lower than predicted.
Fuel was the main reason. Petrol and diesel went up faster than at any time since July 2022, and diesel reached a record price. This follows higher energy costs because of the conflict in the Middle East. Core inflation, which ignores food and energy because they change a lot, stayed at 2.8%.
The Bank of England raised interest rates to 4% on 5 November to try to slow price rises. It warns inflation could reach nearly 5% by the middle of next year.
levels.why: Rising prices leave households with less to spend and keep borrowing costs high.

levels.headline: UK inflation reaches a one-year high of 3.6%
levels.body:
UK inflation rose to 3.6% in October, the highest figure for a year. Inflation measures how fast prices are going up. A rate of 3.6% means an average basket of goods cost 3.6% more than 12 months earlier.
Rising petrol and diesel prices drove the increase. Fuel prices rose at their fastest rate since July 2022 and diesel reached a record high, partly because of the conflict in the Middle East. The underlying rate, which leaves out volatile food and energy costs, was steady at 2.8%.
The Bank of England raised its main interest rate to 4% earlier this month. It expects inflation to come close to 5% by mid-2027, and more rate rises are possible.
levels.why: It means everyday costs are rising faster, and it keeps pressure on interest rates.

levels.headline: Prices are rising faster in the UK, mainly because of fuel
levels.body:
Prices in the UK are rising faster again. In the year to October they went up by 3.6%. This is called inflation, and it is the highest rate for a year.
The biggest reason is the cost of fuel. Petrol and diesel have risen faster than at any time since July 2022. Diesel is at a record price. This is partly linked to the conflict in the Middle East, which has pushed up energy prices. If you take out food and energy, prices rose by 2.8%, the same as before.
The Bank of England wants prices to rise more slowly. It raised its interest rate to 4% this month, and it thinks inflation could get close to 5% next year.
levels.why: When prices rise faster, wages and benefits buy less.

levels.headline: UK prices rose 3.6% in a year, the fastest for 12 months
levels.body:
Prices in the UK are going up faster. In October, they were 3.6% higher than a year before. That is called inflation, and it is the highest in a year.
Most of the rise came from fuel. Petrol and diesel cost more than before, and diesel reached its highest price ever. Energy has got more costly partly because of fighting in the Middle East. When prices for food and energy are left out, inflation was 2.8%, which is the same as last time.
The Bank of England tries to keep prices steady. It raised interest rates to 4% this month. That makes borrowing cost more, which can slow down price rises. It thinks inflation may reach nearly 5% next year.
levels.why: It means money buys a bit less than before, so families may feel worse off.

levels.headline: Prices in the UK are rising faster again
levels.body:
Prices in the UK are going up faster. In the year to October, they rose 3.6%. That is the quickest rise for a year. It is called inflation. It means your money buys a little less than it did.
Most of the rise comes from fuel. Petrol and diesel cost more than at any time since July 2022, and diesel is at a record price. Energy has got more expensive partly because of fighting in the Middle East.
If you leave out food and energy, prices rose by 2.8%, the same as before. The Bank of England has put up interest rates to 4% to try to slow the rises. It thinks inflation could get close to 5% next year.
levels.why: Rising prices make everyday things cost more for families.

levels.headline: Prices in the UK are going up faster
levels.body:
Prices in the UK went up faster in October. A year earlier, things cost less. Now the same things cost 3.6% more on average. This is called inflation. It is the highest it has been for a year.
Fuel is a big reason. Petrol and diesel cost more now. Diesel is at its highest price ever. Fighting in the Middle East has made energy more expensive around the world.
The Bank of England is in charge of keeping prices steady. It sets a price for borrowing money called the interest rate. This month it raised the rate to 4%. The Bank thinks prices might rise even faster next year, by nearly 5%.
levels.why: It can make life costlier for families, and it changes what banks charge for loans.

levels.headline: Things cost more than they did last year
levels.body:
Things in shops and at petrol stations cost more than they did a year ago. In October, prices were 3.6% higher on average. That means something that cost £100 last year costs about £103.60 now. This is called inflation.
Fuel went up the most. Petrol and diesel cost more because oil and gas are more expensive, partly due to fighting in the Middle East.
The Bank of England looks after prices in the UK. It has put up the cost of borrowing money to try to slow things down. The bank thinks prices could rise even faster next year. This can make it harder for families to pay for what they need.
levels.why: It can make it harder for families to afford things.

levels.headline: Prices went up a bit more
levels.body:
Imagine you buy a sweet for £1. Next year the same sweet costs £1.04. The sweet has not changed, but it costs more. When lots of things cost more, we call it inflation.
In the UK, prices went up by 3.6% in a year. That is the most for a whole year. A big reason is that fuel for cars costs more. Fuel is what makes cars and lorries go.
A group of grown-ups at the Bank of England watches prices. They have put up the cost of borrowing money to try to slow the rise. They think prices may go up even more next year. That means pocket money buys a little less.
levels.why: It means families can buy a little less with the same money.

headline: Bank of England raises Bank Rate to 4% by 8 votes to 1, its first rise in over three years, and warns inflation may near 5%

terms.meaning: The Bank of England's interest rate, which influences what banks charge and pay.
The Bank of England group of nine that sets the interest rate.
One hundredth of a percentage point, so 25 basis points is 0.25%.

levels.headline: Bank of England raises Bank Rate to 4% by 8 votes to 1, its first rise in over three years, and warns inflation may near 5%
levels.body:
The Bank of England raised its base rate by 0.25 percentage points to 4% on 5 November, from 3.75%. The Monetary Policy Committee voted 8 to 1. Catherine Mann wanted a bigger rise to 4.25%. It was the first increase since August 2023 and was widely expected.
The Bank says energy-driven inflation linked to the conflict in the Middle East is the cause. It now expects inflation to reach around 5% by the middle of 2027. Official figures published on 18 November showed UK inflation at 3.6% in October.
Governor Andrew Bailey said the increase should not be seen as the first in an inevitable long sequence of hikes, but also said a further rise did not look like the last unless the conflict is resolved. Capital Economics said another rise in December looks increasingly likely. The next decision is on 17 December.
Separately, official data showed the economy grew 0.7% in the third quarter.
levels.why: It sets the cost of mortgages, loans and savings for millions of people.

levels.headline: Bank of England lifts interest rates to 4% for the first time in over three years
levels.body:
The Bank of England raised interest rates from 3.75% to 4% on 5 November. Eight of the nine members of its rate-setting committee backed the move. One, Catherine Mann, wanted a bigger rise to 4.25%. It is the first increase since August 2023.
The Bank is worried about inflation caused by higher energy prices after the Middle East conflict. It now thinks inflation could come close to 5% by the middle of 2027.
Governor Andrew Bailey said the rise should not be seen as the first of a long series. But he also said that unless the conflict is resolved, it does not look like the last. Economists think another increase is likely on 17 December.
The decision came as figures showed the UK economy growing 0.7% in the third quarter.
levels.why: It affects what people pay on mortgages and loans and what they earn on savings.

levels.headline: Bank of England raises interest rates to 4%
levels.body:
The Bank of England put up its main interest rate from 3.75% to 4% on 5 November. This is the first rise in over three years. Eight members of its committee voted for the rise and one wanted it to go higher.
The Bank says prices are being pushed up by more expensive energy because of the conflict in the Middle East. It expects inflation to reach about 5% by the middle of 2027, so it is raising rates to bring it down.
Governor Andrew Bailey said this should not be seen as the start of a long run of rises, but that another one is possible if the conflict goes on. Many economists expect another rise at the next meeting on 17 December.
levels.why: Higher rates make borrowing more expensive but can help savers and slow price rises.

levels.headline: Bank of England puts up interest rates to 4%
levels.body:
The Bank of England has raised the UK's main interest rate to 4%, up from 3.75%. It was the first rise in more than three years. The Bank's committee voted 8 to 1, with one member wanting a bigger increase.
The interest rate is the cost of borrowing money, and it influences what banks charge on mortgages and loans and what they pay savers. The Bank raised it because rising energy costs after the Middle East conflict are pushing up prices. It thinks inflation could near 5% by mid-2027.
Governor Andrew Bailey said the rise is not the start of a long run of rises, but another may be needed if the conflict continues. The next decision is on 17 December.
levels.why: It changes monthly payments for homeowners and borrowers across the country.

levels.headline: The Bank of England raises its interest rate to 4%
levels.body:
The Bank of England has raised the main interest rate in the UK. It went from 3.75% to 4%. This is the first rise in over three years. Eight members of the Bank's rate-setting group voted for it. One wanted a bigger rise.
The interest rate is the price of borrowing money. When it goes up, loans and mortgages tend to cost more. Savers may earn more. The Bank did this because prices are rising faster, mainly because energy costs more after the conflict in the Middle East. It thinks inflation could reach nearly 5% by the middle of next year.
Its boss, Andrew Bailey, said more rises might be needed if the conflict does not end. The next decision is on 17 December.
levels.why: It could make mortgages and loans more costly, but it aims to slow rising prices.

levels.headline: The Bank of England makes borrowing cost more
levels.body:
The Bank of England has put up the interest rate to 4%. It was 3.75% before. This is the first time it has gone up in more than three years. Eight people on the Bank's committee voted yes and one wanted a bigger rise.

headline: UK retail sales volumes rise 0.7% in October as public borrowing comes in at £17.0 billion, below forecast

levels.headline: UK retail sales volumes rise 0.7% in October as public borrowing comes in at £17.0 billion, below forecast
levels.body:
The Office for National Statistics reported on 20 November that retail sales volumes in Great Britain rose 0.7% in October 2026 and were 2.3% higher than a year earlier. Food stores did well as supermarkets reported higher sales of long-life items such as tinned goods and UHT milk, following government advice. Online sales values rose 1.5% on the month.
Public sector borrowing was £17.0 billion in October, below the £18.0 billion forecast but above the £16.2 billion of October 2025. It is the third-highest October figure since monthly records began in 1993. Central government borrowing was £20.8 billion, broadly unchanged, as higher tax receipts were offset by debt interest of £11.2 billion, up from £8.4 billion.
Borrowing in the financial year to October was £111.3 billion, down from £118.6 billion a year earlier, but £3.3 billion above the Office for Budget Responsibility forecast.
levels.why: It shows whether shoppers are still spending and how much pressure there is on the public finances.

headline: Missiles fall in Poland during massive Russian attack on Ukraine; Tusk calls it a provocation and NATO's Rutte condemns 'grave violations'

levels.headline: Missiles fall in Poland during massive Russian attack on Ukraine; Tusk calls it a provocation and NATO's Rutte condemns 'grave violations'
levels.body:
Poland said missiles and a drone came down on its territory on 20 November during a major overnight Russian attack on Ukraine. Poland's defence minister said a Kh-101 cruise missile landed near Nowy Lipowiec, about 60 km from the Ukrainian border, and another missile and a jet-powered drone fell at two other places. No injuries or damage to critical infrastructure were reported.
Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said Russia fired more than 400 attack drones and over 110 missiles. Euronews also reported strikes on Kyiv that killed six people and damaged two bridges.
Prime Minister Donald Tusk called it a Russian provocation, suggesting the timing may be linked to military exercises on Polish territory, and convened ministers, military and intelligence chiefs. NATO Secretary General Mark Rutte condemned what he called grave violations of Polish airspace. Ukraine's foreign minister also condemned it. The Kremlin's response was not reported in the sources.
levels.why: Poland is a NATO member, so any attack on its territory risks drawing the alliance further into the war.

levels.headline: Anthropic ends first week as a listed company at $88.91, above its $83 IPO price, as Nvidia falls 14% on SEC accounting report
levels.body:
Anthropic shares closed at $88.91 on Friday 20 November, about 7% above the $83 IPO price but well below the $97.17 close on the first day. The stock fell around 9% on Friday, the second day of trading. Anthropic raised $93.5 billion in total once underwriters exercised their greenshoe option.
The listing came as AI shares sold off. CNBC reported that Nvidia fell 14% after a Reuters report that the US Securities and Exchange Commission is examining its accounting; CNBC said the scope of the review is not yet clear. AMD fell more than 13%.
Analysts offered several explanations: that the listing was a cash-out moment for AI investors, that Nvidia's problems weighed on the sector, and that rate worries added to the pressure. The S&P 500 fell 3.7% and the Nasdaq 5.28% on Friday, and the Nasdaq is now lower for 2026.

headline: Trump returns from China with trade, Taiwan and tech tensions unresolved after first three-way meeting with Xi and Putin

levels.headline: Trump returns from China with trade, Taiwan and tech tensions unresolved after first three-way meeting with Xi and Putin
levels.body:
President Donald Trump returned from a four-day Asia trip with few concrete results. The leaders of the United States, China and Russia met together for the first time in Shenzhen around the APEC summit, held from 17 to 19 November. They reaffirmed an interest in reducing nuclear risks and in raising oil production, but made little progress on regional disputes.
Mr Trump and Xi Jinping held their third bilateral summit of the year, but little was disclosed publicly about tariffs, rare earths beyond a January deadline or tech competition. An earlier trade truce runs to January 2027 and a planned $30 billion-for-$30 billion tariff cut is still not in effect. Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent said there would be no change to chip export policy and that Mr Trump drew a very firm line at Nvidia's H200 chips.
Back at the White House, Mr Trump defended his ties with Xi and Vladimir Putin, saying Mr Putin wants to end the Ukraine war through diplomacy. European leaders have rejected a "Yalta 2.0" settlement for Ukraine.
levels.why: The relationship between the world's three biggest military powers shapes trade, the Ukraine war and prices.

The leaders agreed to reduce nuclear risks and to boost oil production. They did not announce much else. A trade truce between the US and China, which keeps tariffs lower, runs until January 2027. A planned cut in tariffs has not yet taken effect, and little was said about it.
US Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent said there will be no change to rules on selling advanced chips to China. Mr Trump defended his ties with both men. European leaders have rejected what they call a "Yalta 2.0" deal for Ukraine.
levels.why: The outcome affects trade between the US and China and the future of the war in Ukraine.

levels.headline: Trump meets Xi and Putin but few deals are made
levels.body:
US President Donald Trump has returned from a four-day trip to Asia. In China he met Xi Jinping, the Chinese leader, and Vladimir Putin, the Russian leader, all at the same time. It was the first time the three had met like this.
They said they wanted to lower the risk of nuclear weapons and to make more oil. But there were few big agreements. The US and China have a truce on tariffs, which are taxes on goods from other countries. It lasts until January 2027. A plan to cut some of the tariffs has still not started.
Mr Trump said Mr Putin wants to end the war in Ukraine by talking. European leaders do not want a deal about Ukraine to be made without them.
levels.why: It affects trade, prices and the war in Ukraine.

levels.headline: Trump met China's and Russia's leaders but made few deals
levels.body:
US President Donald Trump went to China for four days. He met China's leader, Xi Jinping, and Russia's leader, Vladimir Putin. It was the first time the three leaders had met together.
They said they wanted fewer nuclear weapon risks, and more oil. But they did not agree many big things. The US and China have a pause in a fight over tariffs. Tariffs are taxes on goods bought from other countries. The pause lasts until January 2027. A plan to cut some of those taxes has still not started.
Mr Trump says Mr Putin wants to end the war in Ukraine by talking. Leaders in Europe have said they do not want a deal about Ukraine without them.
levels.why: It matters for prices in shops, for jobs, and for the war in Ukraine.

levels.headline: Trump meets Xi and Putin in China, with few deals
levels.body:
US President Donald Trump has come back from a four-day trip to Asia. In China he met Xi Jinping and Vladimir Putin together. It was the first time the three leaders had met like this.

levels.headline: The leaders of three big countries met
levels.body:
The leaders of the United States, China and Russia met in China this week. They are Donald Trump, Xi Jinping and Vladimir Putin. It was the first time all three had sat down together.
They talked about trade. Trade means buying and selling things between countries. The US and China have a pause in a fight over tariffs, which are taxes on goods from other countries. The pause lasts until January 2027. They also said they wanted fewer risks from nuclear weapons.
But they did not agree many big things. Mr Trump says Mr Putin wants to end the war in Ukraine by talking. Leaders in Europe want to be part of any deal about Ukraine.
levels.why: It affects the price of goods and whether wars can be ended.

levels.headline: Three world leaders met but did not agree much
levels.body:
Three very powerful leaders met in China this week. They were the president of the United States, Donald Trump, the president of China, Xi Jinping, and the president of Russia, Vladimir Putin. They had never all met together before.
They talked about trade, which means buying and selling things. They also talked about nuclear weapons, which are very dangerous. They said they wanted to make the world safer. But they did not agree on many big things.
Mr Trump says Mr Putin wants the war in Ukraine to end through talking. Leaders in Europe want a say in any deal about Ukraine. They think it is their business too.
levels.why: It matters because these leaders can change how safe and how rich the world is.

levels.headline: Three big leaders met but did not agree much
levels.body:
Imagine the three biggest children in the school meet in the playground. They talk for a long time. Everyone watches to see what will happen. At the end, they say they will try to be kind, but they do not agree on much.
That is a bit like what happened this week. The leaders of the United States, China and Russia met in China. They are Donald Trump, Xi Jinping and Vladimir Putin. They talked about trade and about nuclear weapons.
They did not agree on many big things. Mr Trump says Mr Putin wants the war in Ukraine to end. Leaders in Europe want to help decide how it ends.
levels.why: It matters because big leaders' choices can change life for many people.

headline: Iran readies more than 14 tankers at Kharg Island to test US oil blockade as Trump says he wants a 'real deal'

terms.meaning: Stopping ships or goods from entering or leaving a place.
A narrow sea passage through which much of the world's oil is shipped.
Photographs of the Earth taken from space.

levels.headline: Iran readies more than 14 tankers at Kharg Island to test US oil blockade as Trump says he wants a 'real deal'
levels.body:
Iran has gathered more than 14 oil tankers at Kharg Island in what looks like a convoy preparing to try to break the US naval blockade of its oil exports, Euronews reported on 20 November, citing satellite imagery and ship-tracking data. CNBC has reported that the blockade began in mid-April.
Euronews said the blockade is putting mounting financial pressure on Tehran. It also said President Donald Trump, during his Asia trip, signalled little urgency on Iran and suggested the issue would not be addressed until next year.
Speaking at the White House after returning from the trip, Mr Trump accused Iran of dishonesty in negotiations and called for a "real deal". Reporting is conflicting about whether talks are happening: Mr Trump says they are, while Iran has denied direct negotiations. Earlier threats to seize Kharg Island did not lead to action, and no agreement has been reported.
levels.why: It could decide whether Middle East oil flows freely, which affects fuel prices around the world.

levels.headline: Iran prepares tanker convoy to test US blockade of its oil exports
levels.body:
More than 14 oil tankers have been positioned at Iran's Kharg Island oil hub, ready to leave in what appears to be an attempt to break the US naval blockade of Iranian oil, Euronews reported on 20 November. It cited satellite images and ship-tracking data. The blockade began in mid-April.
The report said the blockade is putting growing financial pressure on Iran, and that Donald Trump indicated during his trip to Asia that he is in no hurry on Iran. He suggested it would wait until next year.
At the White House, Mr Trump accused Iran of dishonesty in talks and said he wants a "real deal". Iran has denied holding direct negotiations. No agreement has been reported.
levels.why: The standoff keeps oil markets on edge and affects UK petrol and energy prices.

levels.headline: Iran lines up oil tankers to challenge US blockade
levels.body:
Iran has lined up more than 14 oil tankers at Kharg Island, its main oil export hub. Satellite pictures and ship-tracking data suggest they could be preparing a convoy to test the US navy blockade that has disrupted Iranian oil exports since mid-April, Euronews reported.
The blockade is putting growing financial pressure on Iran. President Donald Trump has suggested he is in no rush to deal with the issue and that it could wait until next year.
Speaking at the White House on his return from Asia, Mr Trump accused Iran of dishonesty in talks and called for a "real deal". Iran has said it is not holding direct negotiations, and no agreement has been reported.
levels.why: It affects the price of oil, and so petrol and heating bills.

levels.headline: Iran prepares tanker convoy to test US oil blockade
levels.body:
Iran has gathered more than 14 oil tankers at Kharg Island, its main oil port. Satellite images and ship data suggest this may be a convoy that will try to break a US naval blockade of Iranian oil, which began in mid-April, Euronews reported.
The blockade is putting financial pressure on Iran. Donald Trump has indicated he is not in a hurry to settle the dispute, and suggested it might wait until next year.
After returning from Asia, Mr Trump told the White House that Iran was being dishonest in negotiations and that he wants a "real deal". Iran has denied direct talks. No deal has been reported, and the standoff continues.
levels.why: It matters for world oil supplies and for prices at the pump.

levels.headline: Iran gets oil ships ready to challenge the US
levels.body:
Iran has put more than 14 oil tankers at Kharg Island, its main oil port. Pictures from space and ship-tracking data suggest the ships may be about to sail together as a convoy. The aim could be to break a blockade by the US navy. A blockade is when ships are stopped from entering or leaving. This one has disrupted Iranian oil exports since mid-April.
The blockade is costing Iran a lot of money. President Donald Trump has said little about it recently and may leave it until next year.
This week he said Iran has not been honest in talks and he wants a "real deal". Iran says it is not holding direct talks.
levels.why: It could affect how much oil reaches the world and what petrol costs.

levels.headline: Iran prepares a group of oil ships to test a US blockade
levels.body:
Iran has gathered more than 14 oil ships, called tankers, at an island called Kharg. This is where Iran loads oil onto ships. Pictures taken from space show them. They may be getting ready to sail out together.
The US navy has been stopping Iranian oil ships since mid-April. This is called a blockade. It means Iran cannot sell much oil, so it is losing money.
President Donald Trump says Iran is not being honest in talks. He wants what he calls a "real deal". Iran says it is not talking to the US directly. No deal has been agreed.
levels.why: If the oil cannot get out, prices can go up around the world.

levels.headline: Iran readies oil ships to test a US blockade
levels.body:
Iran has gathered more than 14 oil ships, called tankers, at its island port of Kharg. Pictures from space and ship-tracking data show them. They may be about to sail out together.
Since mid-April, the US navy has been blocking Iranian oil exports. This is called a blockade. It is costing Iran a lot of money.
The US president, Donald Trump, says Iran has not been honest in talks and he wants a "real deal". He has hinted that he may leave the issue until next year. Iran says it is not holding direct talks with the US. No deal has been agreed.
levels.why: If oil cannot get out, prices can rise around the world.

levels.headline: Iran gets its oil ships ready to sail
levels.body:
Iran sells oil to other countries. It loads the oil onto big ships called tankers. Since April, the US navy has been stopping those ships from leaving. This is called a blockade. It means Iran is losing a lot of money.
Now Iran has put more than 14 tankers at an island called Kharg. Pictures taken from space show them. They may sail out together to see if the US will stop them.
The US president, Donald Trump, says Iran has not been honest in talks. He wants a "real deal". Iran says it is not talking to the US directly. No deal has been agreed.
levels.why: It matters because oil is used for petrol, and fights over it can raise prices.

levels.headline: Iran puts a lot of oil ships in one place
levels.body:
Oil is a thick liquid that is used to make petrol for cars. Iran has lots of oil. It sells it to other countries by loading it onto big ships.
Since April, the US navy has been stopping those ships. Iran is not happy about it. Now Iran has put more than 14 oil ships together at one island called Kharg. People think they may try to sail out all at once.
The president of America, Donald Trump, says Iran is not telling the truth in talks. He wants a "real deal". Iran says it is not talking to him directly. Nobody has agreed anything yet.
levels.why: It could change how much petrol costs.

levels.headline: Ships waiting to leave a port
levels.body:
Imagine a long line of ships all waiting at a port. They are full of oil. But a guard is outside the port and will not let them leave. That is a bit like what is happening with Iran.
Iran sells oil. Since April, the American navy has been stopping Iran's ships from sailing out. Now Iran has gathered more than 14 big ships together. They may try to all go at the same time.
The president of the United States, Donald Trump, says Iran has not been honest in talks. He wants a proper deal. Iran says it is not talking to him directly. Nothing is agreed yet.
levels.why: It matters because oil makes cars go, and fights over it can make it cost more.

headline: Oil heads for third weekly fall with Brent near $90 as Gulf exports recover

terms.meaning: The main international benchmark price for oil.
A narrow sea passage between Iran and Oman through which a large share of the world's oil travels.
When more is supplied than is needed.

levels.headline: Oil heads for third weekly fall with Brent near $90 as Gulf exports recover
levels.body:
Brent crude traded at around $90 to $92 a barrel on 20 November. Trading Economics put Brent at $90.06, down 2.09% on the day, while CNBC reported $92.22 in the afternoon in New York. Brent was on course for a decline of nearly 4% on the week, its third weekly fall in a row.
The market is pricing in a surplus because crude shipments through the Strait of Hormuz have returned to roughly pre-war levels. On 16 November CNBC reported US crude at about $85 a barrel as Middle East exports recovered.
Some risk remains. Reports of possible further US strikes on Iran have kept some support under prices, and Iran is preparing a tanker convoy to test the US blockade of its exports. Oil costs feed directly into inflation: UK motor fuel inflation reached its highest since July 2022 in October, and the Bank of England has linked its forecast of inflation near 5% to energy prices.
levels.why: Oil prices drive petrol, heating and food costs, and so inflation and interest rates.

levels.headline: Oil prices fall for a third week as Middle East supplies return
levels.body:
Brent crude, the main global oil price, was around $90 to $92 a barrel on 20 November. Trading Economics had it at $90.06, down 2.09% on the day, and CNBC reported $92.22 during the afternoon. It is set to finish the week nearly 4% lower, the third weekly fall in a row.
Traders now expect more oil than the world needs, because ships carrying crude through the Strait of Hormuz are back to roughly pre-war levels. On 16 November US crude was about $85 a barrel.
Reports of possible new US strikes on Iran are still holding prices up a little. Higher oil costs have pushed up UK petrol and diesel prices, and the Bank of England has pointed to energy costs in explaining why it raised interest rates.
levels.why: Lower oil prices could eventually ease pressure on petrol prices and inflation.

levels.headline: Oil prices set for a third weekly fall
levels.body:
Oil prices are heading for their third weekly fall in a row. Brent crude, the main global benchmark, was between $90 and $92 a barrel on 20 November, down nearly 4% over the week.
The main reason is that oil shipments through the Strait of Hormuz, a narrow sea route in the Gulf, have returned to about the level seen before the war in the Middle East. Traders now expect more oil to be available than the world needs, which pushes prices down.
Some risk remains. Reports of possible new US strikes on Iran have stopped prices from falling further. Oil costs matter because they affect petrol, heating and many other prices. UK petrol and diesel prices have recently been rising.
levels.why: If oil stays cheaper, petrol and energy prices could ease, which helps inflation.

levels.headline: Oil heads for third weekly fall as exports from the Middle East recover
levels.body:
Oil prices are falling for a third week in a row. Brent crude, the main international price, traded at about $90 to $92 a barrel on 20 November. That is nearly 4% lower than a week earlier.
Shipments through the Strait of Hormuz, a narrow channel in the Gulf through which much of the world's oil passes, are back near their level before the war in the Middle East. That has led traders to expect a surplus, meaning more oil than is needed.
Prices have not fallen further because of reports that the US may strike Iran again. Oil prices matter because they feed into the cost of petrol, heating and transport, and so into inflation.
levels.why: Oil is a key part of the cost of living and of the Bank of England's decisions.

levels.headline: Oil prices are falling again
levels.body:
The price of oil has fallen for the third week running. A barrel of Brent crude, the main world price, cost about $90 to $92 on 20 November. That is nearly 4% less than a week earlier.
One reason is that ships can carry oil through the Strait of Hormuz again. This is a narrow stretch of sea in the Gulf. A lot of the world's oil goes through it. Shipments there are now close to what they were before the war in the Middle East. That means there may be more oil than people need, so prices drop.
But prices have not fallen further because of worries that the US might strike Iran. Oil matters because it helps set the price of petrol and many other goods.
levels.why: Cheaper oil can lead to lower petrol prices and slower price rises.

levels.headline: The price of oil keeps falling
levels.body:
The price of oil has gone down for three weeks in a row. A barrel of oil cost about $90 to $92 on 20 November. That is nearly 4% less than a week before.
Oil comes from the Middle East in big ships. Many of them go through a narrow sea route called the Strait of Hormuz. For a while, the war in the Middle East made this harder. Now the ships are moving as before. So there is more oil on the market, and the price goes down.
The price has not fallen further because people worry the US may attack Iran again. Oil matters because it is used to make petrol and many other things.
levels.why: It can change how much petrol and heating cost.

levels.headline: Oil falls for a third week as ships move again
levels.body:
The price of oil has fallen for the third week in a row. A barrel of Brent crude, the main world price, cost about $90 to $92 on 20 November. That is nearly 4% less than a week before.
The reason is that oil ships can sail through the Strait of Hormuz again. This is a narrow sea route in the Gulf that carries a lot of the world's oil. Shipments are back close to what they were before the war in the Middle East. With more oil on the market, prices fall.
Prices have not fallen further because people worry the US may strike Iran again. Oil affects petrol and many other prices.
levels.why: Cheaper oil can lead to cheaper petrol and slower price rises.

levels.headline: Oil is getting cheaper
levels.body:
Oil is used to make petrol for cars and lorries. The price of oil has gone down for three weeks in a row. By Friday 20 November, a barrel cost about $90 to $92. That is nearly 4% less than a week before.
The reason is that ships are carrying oil again from the Middle East. A narrow sea route called the Strait of Hormuz had been hard to use because of a war. Now it is working almost normally. When there is more oil to sell, the price goes down.
But some people worry that the US may attack Iran. That has stopped prices from falling more. If oil stays cheap, petrol might cost less soon.
levels.why: It could make petrol and bills cheaper.

levels.headline: Oil costs a bit less than before
levels.body:
Oil is a thick liquid from under the ground. It is used to make petrol for cars. The price of oil has gone down three weeks in a row. This week it was about 4% lower.
Oil travels in big ships. Many ships go through a narrow stretch of sea called the Strait of Hormuz. A war in the Middle East made it hard for them. Now the ships are moving again. When there is plenty of oil to buy, it costs less.
Some people still worry that there could be more fighting. That has stopped the price from falling more. If oil gets cheaper, petrol might too.
levels.why: It could make petrol and heating cheaper.

levels.headline: Oil is a bit cheaper this week
levels.body:
Imagine a shop that sells apples. If lots of apples arrive, the shop sells them for less. If only a few arrive, they cost more.
Oil works a bit like that. The ships that carry oil had trouble getting through a narrow sea route because of a war. Now they are moving again, so there is more oil to buy. This week the price fell for the third week in a row.
Oil is used to make petrol for cars. If it keeps getting cheaper, then petrol might cost less too. But some grown-ups worry there may be more fighting, and that could push prices up again.
levels.why: It could mean cheaper petrol and lower bills for families.

headline: COP31 talks in Antalya run past deadline in deadlock as fossil fuel phase-out wording is dropped

terms.meaning: The annual UN climate conference, short for Conference of the Parties.
Moving to clean energy fairly, so workers and communities are not left behind.
Money from richer countries to help poorer ones cut emissions and adapt.

levels.headline: COP31 talks in Antalya run past deadline in deadlock as fossil fuel phase-out wording is dropped
levels.body:
UN climate talks in Antalya, Turkey, failed to reach a deal on their last scheduled day, 20 November, and negotiators are expected to continue into the weekend, Euronews reported. A final outcome had not been reported at the time of writing.
Talks are deadlocked over four issues: a concrete roadmap to phase out fossil fuels, making sure a 35% by 2035 electrification goal relies on clean energy, delivering climate finance, and guaranteeing a just transition for workers.
Australia, which chairs the negotiations, published a draft on 19 November that removed earlier wording calling on countries to accelerate the phase-out of coal, oil and gas. Campaigners rejected the draft, and some urged countries in the Global South to walk away. They also noted that the United States was absent for a second year in a row.
Side deals were signed in Antalya, including a seven-gigawatt solar and wind plan with China.
levels.why: Whether countries agree to move away from fossil fuels shapes future energy prices and the pace of climate change.

levels.headline: COP31 climate talks in Turkey miss deadline as countries clash over fossil fuels
levels.body:
The UN climate summit in Antalya, Turkey, did not reach agreement by its final scheduled day on 20 November. Negotiators are expected to keep working into the weekend. No final outcome was reported when this was written.
Four issues are blocking progress: a roadmap to phase out fossil fuels, making sure a target to increase electricity use by 35% by 2035 is met with clean energy, money for climate action, and fair treatment for workers affected by the switch.
Australia, chairing the talks, published a draft on 19 November that dropped language on speeding up the end of coal, oil and gas. Campaigners rejected it, and some called on poorer countries to walk away. The United States is absent for the second year in a row.
levels.why: It affects how fast the world moves away from coal, oil and gas.

levels.headline: Climate talks in Turkey miss deadline
levels.body:
The UN climate summit known as COP31, held in Antalya, Turkey, has gone past its final scheduled day without a deal. Negotiators are expected to work into the weekend. No result had been reported when this was written.
Countries are stuck on four main points: a plan to phase out fossil fuels, making sure a target for more electric power by 2035 uses clean energy, money to help poorer countries, and fairness for workers whose jobs change.
Australia, which is leading the talks, published a draft on 19 November that left out earlier wording on speeding up the end of coal, oil and gas. Campaigners rejected the draft. The United States did not attend for the second year running.
levels.why: The outcome affects how quickly countries cut pollution and who pays for it.

levels.headline: COP31 talks overrun as countries disagree on fossil fuels
levels.body:
The COP31 climate conference in Antalya, Turkey, has overrun its final scheduled day. Negotiators are expected to carry on into the weekend, and no final deal had been reported.
The main disagreements are over a roadmap to phase out fossil fuels, making sure an electricity target for 2035 relies on clean energy, climate finance, which is money for poorer countries, and a just transition, which means a fair change for workers.
A draft published by the Australian chair on 19 November took out earlier wording about speeding up the phase-out of coal, oil and gas. Campaigners criticised it. The United States was absent again this year. Some smaller deals were signed in Antalya, including a China-backed solar and wind plan.
levels.why: It shapes how fast the world cuts the pollution that causes climate change.

levels.headline: Climate talks in Turkey go past their deadline without a deal
levels.body:
World leaders and officials are meeting in Antalya, Turkey, for a UN climate conference called COP31. It was meant to end on Friday 20 November, but no deal was ready. They are expected to keep talking over the weekend.
They disagree on four big things. One is a plan to stop using coal, oil and gas. Another is making sure clean power is used to meet a goal for 2035. A third is money for poorer countries to cope with climate change. The fourth is making the change fair for workers.
Australia, which chairs the talks, took words about ending fossil fuels out of its draft. Campaign groups were not happy. The United States did not send anyone this year.
levels.why: It will decide how quickly the world cuts pollution that is warming the planet.

levels.headline: Climate talks in Turkey have not finished
levels.body:
Leaders from many countries are in Antalya, Turkey, for a big climate meeting called COP31. They want to agree on how to deal with climate change. The meeting should have ended on Friday 20 November, but they could not agree. So they will keep talking.
They disagree about a few things. One is whether to say clearly that the world should stop using coal, oil and gas. Another is who should pay to help poorer countries. A third is how to look after workers whose jobs change.
Australia, which is leading the meeting, left out some strong words about ending fossil fuels. Groups who care about nature were upset. The United States did not come.
levels.why: The decisions will affect our planet and the energy we use.

levels.headline: Climate talks in Turkey go past their deadline
levels.body:
Countries are meeting in Antalya, Turkey, for a United Nations climate meeting called COP31. It should have ended on Friday 20 November, but there was no deal. They will keep talking over the weekend.
They disagree about four things. One is a plan to stop using coal, oil and gas. Another is making sure clean power is used to meet a goal for 2035. A third is money to help poorer countries. The fourth is making the change fair for workers.
Australia, which leads the talks, took strong words about ending fossil fuels out of its draft. Campaigners were not happy. The United States did not send anyone.
levels.why: The outcome will decide how quickly countries try to slow climate change.

levels.headline: Leaders cannot agree on how to help the planet
levels.body:
Many countries are meeting in Turkey to talk about climate change. This is when the Earth gets warmer, often because of burning coal, oil and gas. The meeting is called COP31. It was meant to finish on Friday 20 November, but the countries could not agree.
They are arguing about a few things. Should they say clearly that coal, oil and gas must stop being used? Who should pay to help poorer countries? How can they help workers whose jobs will change?
The leader of the talks, from Australia, took out some strong words about ending fossil fuels. Some people who care about nature were upset. The United States did not come.
levels.why: It decides how fast the world tries to stop the planet getting warmer.

levels.headline: Countries are still arguing about how to protect the Earth
levels.body:
The Earth is getting warmer. Many people think burning coal, oil and gas is a big reason why. This week, countries are meeting in Turkey to talk about what to do. It is called COP31.
They were meant to finish on Friday. But they could not agree. Some countries want to say clearly that coal, oil and gas must stop. Others do not. They also argue about money. Rich countries are asked to help poorer ones.
They will keep talking this weekend. Some people who care about nature are upset because strong words were taken out. The United States did not come.
levels.why: It matters because the choices will affect the world you grow up in.

levels.headline: Grown-ups are arguing about how to keep the Earth cool
levels.body:
Imagine a class project where everyone has to agree on a plan. Some children want a bold plan. Some do not. The teacher says time is up, but nobody has agreed.
That is a bit like what is happening in Turkey. Many countries are talking about how to stop the Earth getting too warm. It was meant to finish on Friday, but they did not agree. They will keep talking at the weekend.
They argue about whether to stop using coal, oil and gas, and about who should pay to help poorer countries. Some people feel sad that strong words were taken out. They want the grown-ups to try harder.
levels.why: It is about looking after the Earth for everyone.

headline: Eurozone inflation hits 4%, a three-year high, as energy costs surge and markets expect an ECB rate rise in December

terms.meaning: The 20 or so EU countries that use the euro.
The ECB's main interest rate, paid on banks' deposits with it.
Inflation leaving out food and energy.

levels.headline: Eurozone inflation hits 4%, a three-year high, as energy costs surge and markets expect an ECB rate rise in December
levels.body:
Eurozone inflation rose to 4% in October, its highest in more than three years, as energy bills kept pushing up the cost of living, Euronews reported. Energy prices were 20.8% higher than a year earlier, while core inflation held at 2.5%. Germany was an exception, with inflation falling to 2.8% mainly because of a fuel tax cut.
The European Central Bank kept its deposit facility rate at 2.5% on 29 October, after raising it in June and September. Prediction markets give about an 84% chance of a quarter-point rise at its meeting on 16 and 17 December. Christine Lagarde has said she will step down in February, nine months before her term ends.
The European Commission's autumn forecast puts eurozone growth at 1.2% this year and next, and expects EU inflation to peak above 4% around the turn of the year. The October final composite PMI, a survey of business activity, was 51.7, down from 53.1 in September.
levels.why: It shows the energy shock is hitting households across Europe and keeping interest rates rising.

levels.headline: Eurozone prices rise 4% in a year as energy costs soar
levels.body:
Inflation in the countries that use the euro reached 4% in October, the highest in over three years, Euronews reported. Energy cost 20.8% more than a year before. Core inflation, which leaves out energy and food, was 2.5%. Germany's rate fell to 2.8%, helped by a cut in fuel tax.
The European Central Bank held its main interest rate at 2.5% on 29 October after raising it in June and September. Prediction markets see about an 84% chance of another quarter-point rise when it meets on 16 and 17 December. Its president, Christine Lagarde, will step down in February.
The European Commission expects eurozone growth of 1.2% this year and next, and thinks EU inflation will peak above 4% around the start of next year.
levels.why: The cost of energy is squeezing households and could slow the European economy.

levels.headline: Eurozone inflation hits 4%, the highest for three years
levels.body:
Prices in the 20 or so countries that use the euro were 4% higher in October than a year earlier. That is the fastest in more than three years. Energy was the main cause: it cost 20.8% more. Prices excluding energy and food rose 2.5%. Germany bucked the trend, with inflation of 2.8% after a cut in fuel tax.
The European Central Bank kept its main interest rate at 2.5% at the end of October, after raising it twice earlier this year. Markets think there is about an 84% chance it will raise rates again on 16 or 17 December. Christine Lagarde has said she will leave her job as ECB president in February.
The European Commission expects the economy to grow 1.2% this year and next.
levels.why: High energy costs hit households and push interest rates up.

levels.headline: Eurozone inflation reaches 4% as energy bills rise

Inflation in the eurozone, the group of countries that use the euro, rose to 4% in October. That is the highest in over three years. Energy prices were 20.8% higher than a year earlier. Without food and energy, inflation was 2.5%. In Germany it fell to 2.8%, mainly because of a cut in fuel tax.
The European Central Bank, which sets interest rates for the eurozone, held its main rate at 2.5% on 29 October after raising it in June and September. Markets give about an 84% chance of another rise in December. Its president, Christine Lagarde, plans to leave in February.
The European Commission forecasts growth of 1.2% this year and next.
levels.why: It shows that the energy shock is not only a British problem.

levels.headline: Prices in the eurozone are rising faster because of energy
levels.body:
Prices in the countries that use the euro went up 4% in the year to October. This is the fastest rise in more than three years. The main reason is energy. Gas, electricity and fuel cost 20.8% more than a year ago. Without food and energy, prices rose 2.5%. In Germany, prices rose less, by 2.8%, because the government cut a tax on fuel.
The European Central Bank sets interest rates for these countries. It kept its rate at 2.5% on 29 October. It raised it in June and September. Many investors think it will raise it again in December. Its boss, Christine Lagarde, will leave in February.
The EU expects the economy to grow by 1.2% this year and next.
levels.why: Higher prices make life costlier for families across Europe.

levels.headline: Prices in Europe are going up faster
levels.body:
In countries that use the euro, prices are going up faster. In the year to October, they rose 4%. That is the biggest rise in over three years. Energy is the big reason. It costs 20.8% more than a year ago. Germany had a smaller rise, 2.8%, after cutting a tax on fuel.
The European Central Bank looks after interest rates for these countries. Its rate is 2.5%. It was raised twice this year. Many people think it will go up again in December. The bank's boss, Christine Lagarde, will leave her job in February.
Experts think the economy will grow by 1.2% this year and next.
levels.why: It shows how high energy costs are spreading across many countries.

levels.headline: Prices in Europe rise 4% as energy costs jump
levels.body:
In the countries that use the euro, prices went up 4% in the year to October. That is the fastest rise in more than three years. This is called inflation.
The main reason is energy. It costs 20.8% more than a year ago. Without food and energy, prices rose 2.5%. Germany had a smaller rise, of 2.8%, because it cut a tax on fuel.
The European Central Bank sets interest rates for these countries. It kept its rate at 2.5% on 29 October after raising it twice this year. Many investors think it will raise it again in December. Its boss, Christine Lagarde, will leave in February.
levels.why: It shows high energy prices are hurting families across Europe.

levels.headline: Prices in Europe rise because energy costs more
levels.body:
Many countries in Europe use the same money, called the euro. In those countries, prices went up 4% in the year to October. That is more than at any time in the last three years.
The main reason is energy. It costs 20.8% more than a year ago. Germany had a smaller rise, because its government cut a tax on fuel.
A bank called the European Central Bank sets the cost of borrowing for these countries. It put the cost up twice this year. Many people think it will do so again in December. The boss of the bank, Christine Lagarde, will leave in February.
levels.why: It means families in Europe pay more for heating and fuel.

levels.headline: Things cost more in Europe
levels.body:
Lots of countries in Europe use the euro as their money. In those countries, prices rose by 4% in a year. That means things cost more than before. It is the biggest rise for three years.
Energy is the main reason. Gas, electricity and fuel cost about a fifth more than last year. Germany had a smaller rise because it made fuel cheaper by cutting a tax.
A big bank called the European Central Bank sets the cost of borrowing. It has put the cost up twice this year. It may do it again in December. Its boss, Christine Lagarde, is leaving in February.
levels.why: It makes life costlier for families who need to heat their homes.

levels.headline: Prices go up in Europe too
levels.body:
Prices are going up in the UK, and they are going up in Europe too. Many European countries use the euro as their money. There, prices went up 4% in a year. That means something that cost €100 now costs about €104.
Heating and fuel cost much more, about a fifth more than last year. That is the biggest reason. Germany cut a tax on fuel, so prices there went up by less.
A bank looks after the cost of borrowing money for these countries. It might make borrowing cost more in December. This helps to slow prices down, but it can be hard for families who have borrowed.
levels.why: It shows that rising prices are happening across Europe, not just here.
